6.1Symmetry operations, elements and point groups

Decision flow
  1. An action that leaves the molecule apparently unchanged = symmetry operation. The point, line or plane it is performed about = symmetry element
  2. Five kinds: identity $E$ / rotation $C_n$ / reflection $\sigma$ / inversion $i$ / improper rotation $S_n$
  3. The set of symmetry elements a molecule has → its point group (Schoenflies symbol)
OperationElementSymbol
Identitywhole of space$E$
Rotation by 360°/$n$$n$-fold rotation axis$C_n$
Reflectionmirror plane$\sigma$
Inversioncentre of inversion$i$
Rotation by 360°/$n$ + reflection in a plane perpendicular to the axis$n$-fold improper-rotation axis$S_n$

Note: $S_1 = \sigma$ and $S_2 = i$.

Rotation axes

H₂O is unchanged only by the 180° rotation ($C_2$) about the bisector of the HOH angle. NH₃ has a $C_3$ axis with two operations, $C_3$ and $C_3^2$.

With several rotation axes, the one with the largest $n$ is the principal axis (usually $z$). XeF₄ has a $C_4$ principal axis and two sets of perpendicular $C_2'$ and $C_2''$ axes.

Mirror planes

Decision flow
  1. How is the plane oriented relative to the principal axis?
  2. Contains the principal axis → $\sigma_\text{v}$ (vertical)
  3. Perpendicular to the principal axis → $\sigma_\text{h}$ (horizontal)
  4. Contains the principal axis and bisects two $C_2$ axes → $\sigma_\text{d}$ (dihedral)

Inversion and improper rotation

Inversion $i$: every atom is moved through the centre to an equal distance on the opposite side. SF₆ and CO₂ have a centre of inversion; H₂O and tetrahedral molecules do not. Inversion is easily confused with a $C_2$ rotation.

Improper rotation $S_n$: a $C_n$ rotation followed by reflection in a plane perpendicular to the axis. CH₄ has no $C_4$ axis but has three $S_4$ axes.

Example: eclipsed ethane has $E, C_3, 3C_2, \sigma_\text{h}, 3\sigma_\text{v}, S_3$; staggered ethane has $E, C_3, 3C_2, 3\sigma_\text{d}, i, S_6$.

(b) Assigning the point group

Decision flow
  1. Linear? → Yes: has $i$ → $D_{\infty h}$ / no $i$ → $C_{\infty v}$
  2. Two or more $C_n$ with $n>2$? → Yes: has $i$ → $O_\text{h}$ or $I_\text{h}$ / no $i$ → $T_\text{d}$
  3. Pick the highest $C_n$: are there $n$ $C_2$ axes perpendicular to it? → Yes: $D$ groups; No: $C$ groups
  4. $D$ groups: $\sigma_\text{h}$ → $D_{nh}$ / $n\sigma_\text{d}$ → $D_{nd}$ / neither → $D_n$
  5. $C$ groups: $\sigma_\text{h}$ → $C_{nh}$ / $n\sigma_\text{v}$ → $C_{nv}$ / $S_{2n}$ → $S_{2n}$ / none → $C_n$
  6. No rotation axis: $\sigma$ → $C_\text{s}$ / $i$ → $C_\text{i}$ / neither → $C_1$
Point groupSymmetry elementsExamples
$C_1$$E$SiHClBrF
$C_2$$E, C_2$H₂O₂
$C_\text{s}$$E, \sigma$NHF₂
$C_{2v}$$E, C_2, \sigma_\text{v}, \sigma_\text{v}'$SO₂Cl₂, H₂O
$C_{3v}$$E, 2C_3, 3\sigma_\text{v}$NH₃, PCl₃, POCl₃
$C_{\infty v}$$E, 2C_\phi, \infty\sigma_\text{v}$OCS, CO, HCl
$D_{2h}$$E, 3C_2, i, 3\sigma$N₂O₄, B₂H₆
$D_{3h}$$E, 2C_3, 3C_2, \sigma_\text{h}, 2S_3, 3\sigma_\text{v}$BF₃, PCl₅
$D_{4h}$$E, 2C_4, C_2, 2C_2', 2C_2'', i, 2S_4, \sigma_\text{h}, 2\sigma_\text{v}, 2\sigma_\text{d}$XeF₄, trans-[MA₄B₂]
$D_{\infty h}$$E, \infty C_2', 2C_\phi, i, \infty\sigma_\text{v}, 2S_\phi$CO₂, H₂, C₂H₂
$T_\text{d}$$E, 8C_3, 3C_2, 6S_4, 6\sigma_\text{d}$CH₄, SiCl₄
$O_\text{h}$$E, 8C_3, 6C_2, 6C_4, 3C_2, i, 6S_4, 8S_6, 3\sigma_\text{h}, 6\sigma_\text{d}$SF₆

"Tetrahedral" and "octahedral" describe shapes, but the point group is not necessarily $T_\text{d}$ or $O_\text{h}$ (different substituents lower the symmetry). The groups related to the cube are the cubic groups $T_\text{d}$ and $O_\text{h}$. The icosahedral group $I_\text{h}$ occurs for B₁₂ clusters and C₆₀.

6.2Character tables

Decision flow
  1. Open the character table of the point group
  2. Top left = group name; top row = operations (by class); top right = order $h$ of the group
  3. Each row = an irreducible representation (symmetry species); the numbers = characters $\chi$
  4. Right-hand columns: functions belonging to that species ($x,y,z$, rotations $R$, quadratic functions $xy$, $x^2-y^2$ …)
CharacterSignificance
1the orbital is unchanged
−1the orbital changes sign
0the orbital undergoes a more complicated change
$C_{2v}$$E$$C_2$$\sigma_\text{v}(xz)$$\sigma_\text{v}'(yz)$$h=4$
$A_1$1111$z$
$A_2$11−1−1$R_z$
$B_1$1−11−1$x$, $R_y$
$B_2$1−1−11$y$, $R_x$

Example: O2s of H₂O is unchanged by every operation → characters (1,1,1,1) → $A_1$. O2p$_x$ changes sign under $C_2$ and is unchanged under $\sigma_\text{v}(xz)$ → (1,−1,1,−1) → $B_1$. O2p$_y$ → $B_2$.

Labelling rules (Mulliken symbols)

  • A: symmetric under rotation about the principal axis (character +1); B: antisymmetric (−1)
  • E: doubly degenerate; T: triply degenerate (the character under the identity $E$ = the degeneracy)
  • Subscripts 1/2: symmetric/antisymmetric under $\sigma_\text{v}$ (or a perpendicular $C_2$); g/u: symmetric (gerade)/antisymmetric (ungerade) under inversion
$C_{3v}$$E$$2C_3$$3\sigma_\text{v}$$h=6$
$A_1$111$z$
$A_2$11−1$R_z$
$E$2−10$(x,y)$, $(R_x,R_y)$

NH₃: N2p$_z$ is $A_1$; N2p$_x$ and N2p$_y$ together belong to $E$ (doubly degenerate).

Symmetry labelDegeneracy
A, B1
E2
T3

Distinguish italic $E$ (identity operation) from roman E (symmetry species). Degenerate orbitals need at least a $C_3$ axis → triple degeneracy needs a cubic group such as $T_\text{d}$, $O_\text{h}$, $I_\text{h}$ (e.g. the maximum degeneracy in BF₃, $D_{3h}$, is 2).

6.3Polar molecules

Decision flow
  1. Can the molecule have a permanent dipole?
  2. Has a centre of inversion $i$ → nonpolar
  3. Belongs to a $D$ group (has $C_2$ perpendicular to the principal axis) → nonpolar
  4. Cubic groups ($T$, $O$) and $I$ → nonpolar
  5. Otherwise ($C_n$, $C_{nv}$, $C_\text{s}$ …) → may be polar (dipole lies along the axis / in the plane)

Summary: polar molecules belong only to $C_1$, $C_\text{s}$, $C_n$ and $C_{nv}$.

Examples: ruthenocene ($D_{5h}$) is nonpolar. BF₃ ($D_{3h}$) is nonpolar; SF₆ and CCl₄ are nonpolar too.

6.4Chiral molecules

Decision flow
  1. Is there an improper-rotation axis $S_n$? (including $\sigma = S_1$ and $i = S_2$)
  2. No → chiral (not superimposable on its mirror image; optically active)
  3. Yes (including a hidden $S_n$) → achiral

Chiral molecules belong to groups with no improper axis, such as $C_n$ and $D_n$. Examples: CHClFBr ($C_1$), [Mn(acac)₃] ($D_3$).

Caution: even with no mirror plane or inversion centre, a molecule with a higher improper axis such as $S_4$ is achiral.

6.5Molecular vibrations

Decision flow
  1. Number of vibrational modes of a molecule with $N$ atoms
  2. Nonlinear → $3N-6$
  3. Linear → $3N-5$

Example: H₂O ($N$=3) → $3\times3-6 =$ 3 modes (symmetric stretch $\nu_1$, bend $\nu_2$, antisymmetric stretch $\nu_3$). CO₂ (linear) → $3\times3-5 =$ 4 modes.

(a) The exclusion rule

Decision flow
  1. Selection rules: IR active ⇔ the vibration changes the dipole moment (same species as $x,y,z$)
  2. Raman active ⇔ the vibration changes the polarizability (same species as a quadratic function $x^2$, $xy$ …)
  3. Molecule with a centre of inversion $i$ → no mode can be both IR and Raman active (exclusion rule)

CO₂: the symmetric stretch $\nu_1$ does not change the dipole → IR inactive, Raman active. The antisymmetric stretch $\nu_3$ and the bend $\nu_2$ are IR active and Raman inactive.

(b) Information from the symmetries of normal modes

Isomers of [PdCl₂(NH₃)₂]: cis is $C_{2v}$, trans is $D_{2h}$. Pd–Cl stretches: cis gives $A_1$ and $B_2$ (both IR and Raman active); trans gives $A_g$ (Raman only) and $B_{2u}$ (IR only) → in the IR, cis shows two bands and trans one.

(c) Assigning molecular symmetry from vibrational spectra

Count 1 if a displacement vector is unmoved by an operation, −1 if it is reversed, and 0 if it moves to another position; this gives a reducible representation, which is then reduced (→ 6.9). Example: the CO stretches of tetrahedral [Ni(CO)₄] span $A_1 + T_2$ → one IR band ($T_2$) and two Raman bands.

6.6Symmetry-adapted linear combinations (SALCs)

Decision flow
  1. MOs are built only from atomic orbitals (or SALCs) of the same symmetry species
  2. The overlap integral between orbitals of different symmetry is zero

Overlap of an s orbital with a p orbital: nonzero if the p orbital points along the bond, but zero if it is perpendicular (positive and negative contributions cancel).

SALCs of the three H1s orbitals of NH₃: $\phi_1 = \psi_{A1s}+\psi_{B1s}+\psi_{C1s}$ ($A_1$); $\phi_2 = 2\psi_{A1s}-\psi_{B1s}-\psi_{C1s}$ and $\phi_3 = \psi_{B1s}-\psi_{C1s}$ (doubly degenerate $E$).

6.7The construction of molecular orbitals

NH₃: N2s, N2p$_z$ and the $A_1$ H1s SALC give three $a_1$ MOs ($1a_1$ bonding, $2a_1$ almost nonbonding (lone pair), $3a_1$ antibonding). N2p$_x$, N2p$_y$ and the E SALCs give $1e$ (bonding) and $2e$ (antibonding).

H₂O: the H1s SALCs are $\phi_1 = \psi_A+\psi_B$ (species $A_1$) and $\phi_2 = \psi_A-\psi_B$ ($B_2$).

Procedure for building an MO diagram

  • 1. Assign the point group of the molecule
  • 2. Look up the shapes of the SALCs in Resource section 5
  • 3. Arrange the SALCs of each fragment and the atomic orbitals in order of energy (s < p < d)
  • 4. Combine SALCs and atomic orbitals of the same symmetry species to form MOs
  • 5. Estimate relative MO energies from overlap and the energies of the parent orbitals
  • 6. Confirm and revise with computational software

6.8The vibrational analogy

The shapes of SALCs resemble combinations of stretching displacements. Example: the A–B stretches of octahedral AB₆ span $A_{1g} + E_g + T_{1u}$. $A_{1g}$ and $E_g$ are Raman active; $T_{1u}$ is IR active (centre of inversion → exclusion rule).

6.9The reduction of a representation

Decision flow
  1. Apply each operation to the basis (orbitals or displacements) to get the characters $\chi(R)$ of the reducible representation $\Gamma$
  2. Use the reduction formula to find how often each irreducible representation occurs, $c_i$
  3. $c_i = \dfrac{1}{h}\displaystyle\sum_C g(C)\chi_i(C)\chi(C)$ ($h$ = order, $g(C)$ = number of operations in class $C$)

$\Gamma = c_1\Gamma_1 + c_2\Gamma_2 + \cdots$. Example: the three H1s orbitals of NH₃ → characters (3, 0, 1) → $A_1 + E$.

Example (cis-[PdCl₂(NH₃)₂], $C_{2v}$, 5 atoms → 15 displacements): $\chi$ = (15, −1, 1, 5) → $c(A_1) = \frac14(15 - 1 + 1 + 5) =$ 5. Overall $\Gamma = 5A_1 + 2A_2 + 3B_1 + 5B_2$. Removing translations ($A_1+B_1+B_2$) and rotations ($A_2+B_1+B_2$) leaves the vibrations $4A_1 + A_2 + B_1 + 3B_2$.

6.10Projection operators

Decision flow
  1. Choose one basis orbital $\psi$
  2. Apply each operation $R$ and write down the orbital it becomes, $R\psi$
  3. Multiply by the character $\chi_i(R)$ of the target species and sum over all operations: $\phi = \sum_R \chi_i(R)R\psi$
  4. Normalize to get the SALC

Example: Cl σ orbitals $\psi_1$–$\psi_4$ of [PtCl₄]²⁻ ($D_{4h}$) → $\phi(A_{1g}) \propto \psi_1+\psi_2+\psi_3+\psi_4$, $\phi(B_{1g}) \propto \psi_1-\psi_2+\psi_3-\psi_4$, $\phi(E_u) \propto \psi_1-\psi_3,\ \psi_2-\psi_4$. Overall $A_{1g} + B_{1g} + E_u$.

KCKey concepts summary

  • Symmetry operations: $E$, $C_n$, $\sigma$ (v/h/d), $i$, $S_n$; $S_1 = \sigma$, $S_2 = i$.
  • Assign point groups with the decision tree (linear → $D_{\infty h}$/$C_{\infty v}$, cubic → $T_\text{d}$/$O_\text{h}$, then $C_n$ and perpendicular $C_2$, then mirror planes).
  • Character table: 1 = unchanged, −1 = sign change, 0 = moved; character under $E$ = degeneracy (A,B: 1; E: 2; T: 3).
  • Polar: only $C_1, C_\text{s}, C_n, C_{nv}$. Chiral: has no $S_n$ axis.
  • Vibrations: $3N-6$ (linear $3N-5$); IR ⇔ $x,y,z$, Raman ⇔ quadratic functions; centre of inversion → exclusion rule.
  • MOs/SALCs: only orbitals of the same species combine. Reduction formula and projection operators.
